modules.title: Check disinfection calculations and their limits
objectives: Calculate CT from a defined residual and effective contact time.
Distinguish nominal detention time from T10.
Evaluate changing flow, level and chemistry against a supplied criterion.
modules.lesson:
### Define the calculation before using it

This module is study and training material for a non-credit pilot. It is not operating or compliance instruction. All facilities, operators, records and readings described in the examples are fictional. Every numerical process value and comparison criterion is a supplied case assumption, not an authorised operating value.

CT combines a disinfectant concentration with an effective contact time. In the simplified relationship used here, CT = C × T10. With C expressed in mg/L and T10 in minutes, CT is expressed in mg·min/L. The multiplication is straightforward. Establishing that the concentration, time and comparison criterion belong together is the difficult part.

The Ontario source, *Procedure for Disinfection of Drinking Water (Ontario)*, explains the CT concept, T10 and disinfectant-specific treatment requirements. Use it to understand the framework. A real assessment also needs the applicable facility approval, approved disinfection basis and validated calculation procedure. A generic spreadsheet cannot establish which treatment segment, residual location or hydraulic relationship a facility may use.

Before calculating, define the question. Which disinfectant species is being assessed? Which organism and treatment objective apply? Where does the segment begin and end? Is the residual measured at the location specified by the calculation method? What temperature, pH and hydraulic configuration apply during the assessment period?

Chemical dose is not the same as residual. Dose describes disinfectant introduced into the water. Residual describes what remains after reactions and decay. Substituting feed dose for the specified residual can overstate available disinfection. Likewise, total chlorine and free chlorine are different measurements. A free-chlorine calculation cannot accept a total-chlorine reading merely because both instruments display mg/L.

A CT ratio is calculated as assessed CT divided by the applicable comparison criterion. A ratio above unity means the calculated value exceeds that criterion under the stated assumptions. It does not independently prove treatment compliance. Unsupported hydraulic assumptions, an unsuitable criterion or unreliable residual data can invalidate an otherwise correct calculation. CT also does not replace the separate evidence needed for filtration performance or other treatment barriers.

### Build an input register and establish effective time

Nominal detention time is working water volume divided by flow through the segment. It describes a volume-to-flow relationship, not the actual distribution of travel times. Mixing, preferential flow paths, dead zones and inlet or outlet arrangements can cause some water to leave much earlier than the nominal time suggests.

T10 is the travel time associated with the early portion of the flow-through distribution, commonly described as the time by which approximately ten percent of tracer has passed the outlet. That percentage defines the hydraulic statistic; it is not an operating limit. The applicable tracer interpretation and calculation method must come from the accepted hydraulic assessment.

For some configurations, the supported method expresses T10 as nominal detention time multiplied by a baffling factor. Other facilities use a tracer-derived relationship that changes with flow, level or configuration. Do not assume a constant factor simply because the spreadsheet has a cell for one. A factor supported at one configuration may be unsupported with a compartment isolated or a bypass open.

Use an input register like the following when assembling a calculation package. It is a review aid, not a substitute for the facility procedure.

| Input | Record to consult | Reason to question or reject the input |
|---|---|---|
| Disinfectant species and residual | Specified analyser channel, method and quality-control record | Channel measures the wrong species, is stale or failed a check |
| Residual location | Approved segment drawing and sample-point identification | Sample is upstream of the required endpoint or outside the segment |
| Flow through the segment | Relevant flowmeter record and meter status | Plant production flow differs from flow in the assessed branch |
| Working volume | Level record and validated level-volume relationship | Nameplate capacity replaces actual water volume |
| Effective-time relationship | Accepted tracer report or authorised hydraulic basis | Current flow, level or valve arrangement is outside its scope |
| Temperature and pH | Specified measurements for the assessment interval | Measurements are missing, unrepresentative or outside criterion conditions |
| Comparison criterion | Applicable approval and disinfectant-specific procedure | Convenient table entry does not match chemistry or treatment objective |
| Time alignment | Historian configuration, clock checks and sample-delay information | Records describe different process intervals |

For parallel branches, identify the flow and volume of the branch being assessed. Dividing combined tank volume by total flow can conceal a poorly performing branch. Combining branch results or adding segment contributions requires the applicable approved method, not an improvised averaging rule.

Time alignment needs more than matching displayed timestamps. An analyser may receive water through a sample line with transport delay. Its displayed residual can therefore describe water sampled earlier than the displayed flow value. Retain the delay basis and use the facility's validated alignment method. Do not invent a convenient shift to make the data agree.

### Worked example: calculate a supported baseline

All values in this example are supplied assumptions for a fictional training contactor. The fictional case package specifies free chlorine, an endpoint residual and a supported constant baffling factor for the stated steady operating condition. It supplies a comparison criterion solely for practising arithmetic. The criterion is not taken from an Ontario table and must not be reused elsewhere.

The supplied working volume is 600 m³. Flow through the segment is 360 m³/h. The supported baffling factor is 0.40, dimensionless. The relevant free-chlorine residual is 0.90 mg/L. Temperature is 12 °C and pH is 7.2, dimensionless. For this specific fictional combination of disinfectant, chemistry, treatment objective and hydraulic basis, the supplied CT criterion is 30 mg·min/L.

**Step 1: convert flow to a consistent time basis.**

Q = 360 m³/h × 1 h/60 min = 6.00 m³/min.

The factor of 60 min/h is a unit conversion, not an operating value.

**Step 2: calculate nominal detention time from working volume.**

t_nominal = 600 m³ ÷ 6.00 m³/min = 100 min.

This is not yet the effective contact time. Using it directly would assume hydraulic behaviour that the supplied case does not support.

**Step 3: apply the supported hydraulic factor.**

T10 = 100 min × 0.40 dimensionless = 40.0 min.

**Step 4: calculate CT using the specified residual.**

CT = 0.90 mg/L × 40.0 min = 36.0 mg·min/L.

**Step 5: compare with the supplied criterion.**

CT ratio = 36.0 mg·min/L ÷ 30 mg·min/L = 1.20 dimensionless.

CT difference = 36.0 mg·min/L − 30 mg·min/L = 6.0 mg·min/L.

**Answer:** the fictional baseline CT is 36.0 mg·min/L. It exceeds the supplied case criterion by 6.0 mg·min/L, with a ratio of 1.20.

That difference is a calculated margin under the case assumptions. It is not permission to reduce chemical feed or increase production. The calculation has not established the uncertainty in the residual, volume or hydraulic relationship. Nor has it established whether the observed condition represents the limiting condition for the assessment period.

Retain the original residual and flow records, level-to-volume conversion, hydraulic-factor reference, chemistry readings, criterion basis and calculation version. Record which values were measured, which were derived and which were supplied assumptions. A reviewer should be able to reproduce the answer without guessing why a particular input was selected.

### Worked example: reassess changed flow, level and chemistry

This example continues the fictional case. All changed values remain supplied teaching assumptions. The case now specifies a stable working volume of 540 m³ and segment flow of 450 m³/h. Residual remains 0.90 mg/L. The fictional hydraulic assessment explicitly supports the same dimensionless factor of 0.40 at this second stable condition. That support is an assumption of the example, not a general claim that factors remain constant.

Initially, temperature remains 12 °C and pH remains 7.2, dimensionless. The supplied comparison criterion therefore remains 30 mg·min/L for this part of the exercise.

**Step 1: convert the changed flow.**

Q = 450 m³/h × 1 h/60 min = 7.50 m³/min.

**Step 2: calculate the changed nominal detention time.**

t_nominal = 540 m³ ÷ 7.50 m³/min = 72.0 min.

**Step 3: calculate the supported effective time.**

T10 = 72.0 min × 0.40 dimensionless = 28.8 min.

**Step 4: calculate CT at the unchanged residual.**

CT = 0.90 mg/L × 28.8 min = 25.92 mg·min/L.

**Step 5: compare with the unchanged case criterion.**

CT ratio = 25.92 mg·min/L ÷ 30 mg·min/L = 0.864 dimensionless.

CT shortfall = 30 mg·min/L − 25.92 mg·min/L = 4.08 mg·min/L.

**Answer:** CT is 25.92 mg·min/L, below the supplied criterion by 4.08 mg·min/L. The unchanged residual has not preserved CT because effective contact time has decreased.

Now consider a separate chemistry variant at that same changed hydraulic condition. The fictional package supplies a temperature of 6 °C, pH of 7.6, dimensionless, and a new comparison criterion of 36 mg·min/L. This criterion is an invented case input, not a value derived from Ontario requirements. The case still supplies the same measured residual and effective time.

**Step 6: confirm the assessed CT for the chemistry variant.**

CT = 0.90 mg/L × 28.8 min = 25.92 mg·min/L.

**Step 7: compare against the chemistry-matched case criterion.**

CT ratio = 25.92 mg·min/L ÷ 36 mg·min/L = 0.720 dimensionless.

CT shortfall = 36 mg·min/L − 25.92 mg·min/L = 10.08 mg·min/L.

**Answer:** the chemistry variant has the same assessed CT but a lower comparison ratio of 0.720. The relevant criterion changed even though the multiplication inputs did not.

Temperature and pH affect disinfectant effectiveness differently for different disinfectants. Do not transfer a free-chlorine interpretation to another chemical disinfectant. The Ontario *Procedure for Disinfection of Drinking Water (Ontario)* provides the disinfectant-specific framework. The applicable procedure must also govern table selection, rounding and any permitted interpolation.

A useful diagnostic calculation asks what residual would mathematically equal the supplied criterion at the assumed effective time:

C_equivalent = 36 mg·min/L ÷ 28.8 min = 1.25 mg/L.

That is a sensitivity result, not an authorised residual or feed setpoint. It excludes measurement uncertainty, chemical demand, feed-system capability, other water-quality constraints and the approved response procedure. It also assumes that the effective time remains valid. Never turn this rearranged equation directly into an operating adjustment.

### Judge validity and prepare a controlled trial record

Separate three questions in the review: Is the arithmetic correct? Are the inputs supported? Is the comparison criterion applicable? A correct answer to the first question cannot compensate for a failure in either of the others.

A sudden flow or level change is not necessarily represented by a steady-state volume-to-flow calculation. During a transition, water already inside the contactor has experienced an earlier hydraulic condition. A current residual and current flow may not describe the same water history. Use the validated transient assessment method where one exists. If the available method does not cover the transition, identify the assessment as unsupported rather than manufacturing a precise result.

Data gaps need explicit treatment. A flat residual trend could mean stable treatment, but it could also mean a frozen analyser output or a held value during maintenance. Check instrument status, sample flow, maintenance entries and historian quality flags. A nearby grab result can help investigate the discrepancy, but it does not automatically replace the missing continuous record. Any substitution must follow the applicable procedure and preserve the reason for the substitution.

The US EPA publication *Generating high-quality turbidity data* discusses measurement-chain and SCADA data-quality issues. It is United States technical guidance, not Ontario law. Its general lesson about checking the chain from measurement to stored record is useful here, but it does not validate a chlorine analyser or establish an Ontario CT method. The residual instrument's own method, maintenance requirements and facility quality-control procedure govern that assessment.

For a controlled optimisation trial, the draft record should identify the variable being studied, the supported hydraulic envelope and the measurements needed to separate its effect from other changes. Changing flow, tank level and disinfectant feed together makes interpretation difficult. A CT change could result from several causes, and the trial would provide weak evidence about which change mattered.

The trial package must obtain its operating boundaries, authorisations, hold points and response criteria from the applicable approval and validated facility procedures. This training module supplies none. Retain baseline records, actual trial conditions, deviations, raw measurements, calculation versions and reviewer comments. Preserve rejected inputs with the reason for rejection rather than deleting inconvenient evidence.

State conclusions narrowly. A defensible training conclusion says that a specified calculation exceeds or falls below a supplied criterion under listed assumptions. An unsupported condition should be described as unsupported. It should not be labelled a pass simply because an optimistic calculation produces a favourable ratio.

### Common errors

- **Using tank capacity instead of working volume.** Nameplate capacity can include space not occupied by water. This overstates detention time when the current level is lower. Use the validated level-volume relationship for the assessed compartment.
- **Using nominal time as T10.** Volume divided by flow does not establish early breakthrough behaviour. Omitting the supported hydraulic correction can substantially overstate effective time.
- **Mixing favourable readings from different intervals.** A high residual from one period and low flow from another create a condition that may never have existed. Align records using the validated timing basis.
- **Treating every chlorine result as interchangeable.** Free chlorine, total chlorine and applied dose answer different questions. The calculation needs the species and location specified by its method.
- **Keeping the old criterion after chemistry changes.** Correct multiplication does not make an unsuitable comparison valid. Recheck disinfectant, temperature, pH and treatment objective.
- **Hiding uncertainty through rounding.** Early rounding can change a close comparison. Retain calculation precision and apply only the rounding conventions supported by the governing procedure. Displayed decimal places do not create measurement accuracy.

### What to verify before you act

Consult the facility's applicable drinking-water approval instruments, including its Municipal Drinking Water Licence and Drinking Water Works Permit where applicable. Identify the conditions and referenced documents that govern the disinfection assessment. The existence of an approved facility does not mean every spreadsheet or historical practice is an approved calculation method.

Check the current *Procedure for Disinfection of Drinking Water (Ontario)* alongside the facility's approved disinfection design basis and validated CT procedure. Confirm the treatment objective, organism, disinfectant, segment boundaries, residual location and criterion-selection method. Verify how the applicable documents address treatment contributions from separate segments. Do not assume that unlike disinfectants or different organism targets can be combined through a simple sum.

Consult the accepted tracer study or hydraulic assessment. Confirm that the actual flow, level, compartment arrangement and valve status are within the supported configuration. Check the current level-volume relationship against the tank being assessed. A drawing for an earlier configuration is not evidence for a modified contactor.

Review flowmeter verification, analyser quality-control and maintenance records, sample-line information, temperature and pH records, and historian status. Confirm that no maintenance hold, channel substitution or clock discrepancy undermines the selected interval. Retain the underlying records, not only a screenshot of the final ratio.

Before an optimisation trial or any operational response, consult the authorised trial plan, applicable operating procedure and the facility's escalation and response records. Those documents determine who reviews a questionable calculation and what action is permitted. If an input or criterion cannot be substantiated, the training conclusion is that the calculation is not decision-ready. A missing basis is not repaired by choosing a conservative-looking number without an accepted method.

### Fictional worked scenario: reject an unsupported hydraulic factor

The facility, operators, records and readings in this scenario are fictional. Every process value and criterion is a supplied training assumption, not an authorised operating value. This exercise supports a non-credit pilot and is not operating or compliance instruction.

The fictional Maple Reach contactor has a baseline working volume of 480 m³ and segment flow of 240 m³/h. Its specified endpoint free-chlorine residual is 0.75 mg/L. Temperature is 12 °C and pH is 7.2, dimensionless. The case supplies a CT criterion of 28 mg·min/L for its stated treatment objective and chemistry.

The controlled case hydraulic report supports a dimensionless factor of 0.35 at both conditions assessed below. An unsigned spreadsheet instead uses a dimensionless factor of 0.60, with no tracer reference. Reject that spreadsheet factor. A separate total-chlorine reading of 0.95 mg/L is also unsuitable for this free-chlorine calculation.

Baseline arithmetic:

- Q = 240 m³/h × 1 h/60 min = 4.00 m³/min.
- t_nominal = 480 m³ ÷ 4.00 m³/min = 120 min.
- T10 = 120 min × 0.35 dimensionless = 42.0 min.
- CT = 0.75 mg/L × 42.0 min = 31.5 mg·min/L.
- Ratio = 31.5 mg·min/L ÷ 28 mg·min/L = 1.125 dimensionless.

A later stable interval has a supplied working volume of 420 m³ and flow of 300 m³/h. Residual and chemistry are unchanged.

- Q = 300 m³/h × 1 h/60 min = 5.00 m³/min.
- t_nominal = 420 m³ ÷ 5.00 m³/min = 84.0 min.
- T10 = 84.0 min × 0.35 dimensionless = 29.4 min.
- CT = 0.75 mg/L × 29.4 min = 22.05 mg·min/L.
- Ratio = 22.05 mg·min/L ÷ 28 mg·min/L = 0.7875 dimensionless.

**Answer:** the baseline exceeds the supplied criterion; the later interval falls below it. Retain aligned raw records, hydraulic support, chemistry evidence and the rejected spreadsheet with reasons. The Ontario source, *Procedure for Disinfection of Drinking Water (Ontario)*, informs the CT and T10 concepts, not these fictional numerical criteria.

### Frame a trial that can answer a specific question

This module is study and training material, not operating or compliance instruction. The pilot is non-credit. Any plant trial requires the facility's authorization and protection framework. All facilities, operators, records and readings in the examples below are fictional. Numerical criteria and operating values are supplied case assumptions for calculation practice, not authorized values or general requirements.

An optimization trial compares a defined change against a credible baseline while protecting every treatment barrier. Start with a question narrow enough to answer: does a candidate coagulation condition reduce settled-water turbidity under comparable source-water conditions without unacceptable effects on filtration, disinfection or chemical handling? A lower settled-water reading answers only part of that question.

Identify the variable being changed and the variables intended to remain stable. A candidate may change coagulant selection, application point or another authorized treatment condition. If several conditions change together, describe the intervention as a package. Do not claim that one component caused the result unless the comparison can separate its effect.

The baseline must represent the process being compared. Yesterday's best reading is not a baseline. Use the facility's validated sampling plan to identify representative locations, operating states and observation periods. Include variation rather than selecting only quiet periods. Record source turbidity, temperature, pH, alkalinity where relevant, production flow, filters in service, recent backwashes and instrument status.

Define the unit of comparison. It might be a matched operating interval, a filter run or a laboratory screening test. These units answer different questions. A bench-scale result can support a hypothesis, but it cannot establish full-scale hydraulic behaviour or downstream performance.

Separate three statements in the trial record:

- **Observation:** the measured outcome changed during the candidate interval.
- **Association:** the change occurred while the candidate was in use under documented conditions.
- **Causal interpretation:** the evidence supports the candidate, rather than another changing condition, as the explanation.

Repeated comparisons under comparable conditions strengthen interpretation. Where authorized and practicable, a planned return to baseline can help reveal whether an apparent improvement was actually a source-water trend. A return comparison still needs stabilization and equivalent measurement quality. It is not a reason to create unnecessary treatment changes.

### Set acceptance, stop and data-quality criteria in advance

Write the decision rules before collecting candidate results. Distinguish success criteria from operating protection criteria. Success describes the evidence needed to support further evaluation. Stop criteria identify conditions requiring action under the facility's approved trial and response procedures. Data-quality criteria determine whether the evidence can be interpreted at all.

A trial can show an attractive average and still fail its protection criteria. Conversely, invalid measurements can make a trial inconclusive without demonstrating that the treatment itself failed. Keep these outcomes separate in the final recommendation.

Use a register like this when drafting the plan. Entries point to local documents rather than supplying substitute limits.

| Decision item | Define before the trial | Evidence to retain | Effect on interpretation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Primary outcome | Sampling location, metric, comparison basis and prospective acceptance criterion | Raw observations, timestamps and calculation sheet | Determines whether the proposed benefit was observed |
| Coagulation constraints | Applicable facility-approved pH, alkalinity and chemical-use conditions | Results, method records and chemical feed verification | A turbidity improvement does not override an applicable constraint |
| Filter protection | Individual-filter measures and authorized interruption criteria | Turbidity trends, flow, headloss and backwash events | Combined results must not hide a deteriorating filter |
| Disinfection protection | Required review using the approved configuration and hydraulic basis | Residual, temperature, pH, flow and configuration records | An incomplete review prevents an all-barriers success claim |
| Measurement validity | Required checks, allowable data treatment and response to missing data | Instrument checks, maintenance and quality flags | Failed quality checks can make the comparison inconclusive |
| Trial ownership | Authorization, observation coverage, escalation and reversion responsibilities | Signed plan and shift handover | Responsibility remains clear when conditions change |

Specify when observations become eligible for comparison. An upstream change does not instantly reach settled-water, filtered-water and disinfection monitoring points. Base observation windows on the site's documented process response and hydraulic understanding. Do not substitute an assumed travel time for a validated hydraulic assessment.

Define how transient conditions will be handled. Startup, backwash recovery and source-water transitions may require separate analysis. State these rules prospectively. Deleting an inconvenient transient after seeing the result is selection bias unless a documented, independently justified quality rule requires exclusion.

Also define what happens when evidence is unavailable. If a critical analyser becomes unreliable, the plan should refer to the authorized response procedure, including any required pause or reversion. Missing evidence is not evidence of safe performance.

An extension needs its own authorization and rationale. Extending only unsuccessful trials until a favourable result appears makes comparisons misleading. Retain the original planned endpoint and distinguish any additional observations from the initial evaluation.

### Worked example: calculate improvement without overstating causation

The following fictional example uses supplied case assumptions. Four eligible matched observations represent each condition. The draft study plan defines a reduction of at least 20% in arithmetic mean settled-water turbidity as its primary learning criterion. That percentage is an illustrative study criterion, not an Ontario requirement or authorization to change treatment. Separate downstream and data-quality criteria must also be satisfied.

The fictional register contains:

| Matched observation | Baseline settled-water turbidity | Candidate settled-water turbidity |
|---|---:|---:|
| A | 0.80 NTU | 0.60 NTU |
| B | 0.84 NTU | 0.64 NTU |
| C | 0.76 NTU | 0.56 NTU |
| D | 0.80 NTU | 0.60 NTU |

The supplied case states that the observation pairs have comparable source conditions, production flow and filter operating state. Instrument checks passed, and the selected windows follow the documented process-response interval. These are assumptions to verify in a real trial, not conclusions produced by the arithmetic.

**Step 1: total the baseline observations.**

Baseline sum = 0.80 NTU + 0.84 NTU + 0.76 NTU + 0.80 NTU = 3.20 NTU.

**Step 2: calculate the baseline arithmetic mean.**

Baseline mean = 3.20 NTU ÷ 4 = 0.80 NTU.

**Step 3: total the candidate observations.**

Candidate sum = 0.60 NTU + 0.64 NTU + 0.56 NTU + 0.60 NTU = 2.40 NTU.

**Step 4: calculate the candidate arithmetic mean.**

Candidate mean = 2.40 NTU ÷ 4 = 0.60 NTU.

**Step 5: calculate the absolute reduction.**

Absolute reduction = 0.80 NTU − 0.60 NTU = 0.20 NTU.

**Step 6: normalize the reduction to the baseline.**

Relative reduction = (0.20 NTU ÷ 0.80 NTU) × 100% = 25%.

**Step 7: compare with the supplied study criterion.**

Criterion margin = 25% − 20% = 5 percentage points.

**Answer:** the candidate mean is 0.60 NTU, an observed reduction of 0.20 NTU or 25%. It meets the supplied primary learning criterion. It does not, by itself, demonstrate overall trial success or prove causation.

An arithmetic mean can hide short deterioration events. Review the underlying sequence and the prospectively selected peak, duration or variability measures. Do not add a new favourable metric after the primary result is known and present it as the original test.

Four matched observations also do not establish that the effect will persist across seasonal conditions. High-frequency readings may be strongly related to adjacent readings, so thousands of SCADA points do not necessarily represent thousands of independent comparisons. Avoid claims of statistical certainty without a suitable analysis.

If source turbidity fell during the candidate interval, the arithmetic would remain correct but the causal interpretation would weaken. Report the observed reduction, identify the source change and seek a better comparison. Retain both favourable and unfavourable eligible observations, the matching rationale, raw exports, quality checks and the calculation version.

### Worked example: distinguish chemical savings from lower production

Chemical consumption needs a consistent basis. A decrease in kilograms per day can result from treating less water rather than improving chemical efficiency. Compare mass per treated volume, and establish whether the recorded mass means commercial product, dry material or active-equivalent chemical. Those bases are not interchangeable.

For this fictional example, supplied reconciled records show baseline active-equivalent chemical use of 216 kg/d at 12,000 m³/d and candidate use of 180 kg/d at 9,000 m³/d. Both masses use the same active-equivalent basis and align with their respective daily flow totals. These are case inputs, not recommended doses or production conditions.

**Step 1: convert baseline mass to milligrams per day.**

Baseline mass = 216 kg/d × 1,000,000 mg/kg = 216,000,000 mg/d.

**Step 2: convert baseline water volume to litres per day.**

Baseline volume = 12,000 m³/d × 1,000 L/m³ = 12,000,000 L/d.

**Step 3: calculate baseline mass per treated volume.**

Baseline normalized use = 216,000,000 mg/d ÷ 12,000,000 L/d = 18 mg/L.

**Step 4: convert candidate mass and volume.**

Candidate mass = 180 kg/d × 1,000,000 mg/kg = 180,000,000 mg/d.

Candidate volume = 9,000 m³/d × 1,000 L/m³ = 9,000,000 L/d.

**Step 5: calculate candidate mass per treated volume.**

Candidate normalized use = 180,000,000 mg/d ÷ 9,000,000 L/d = 20 mg/L.

**Step 6: calculate the change in daily consumption.**

Daily mass reduction = 216 kg/d − 180 kg/d = 36 kg/d.

Relative daily mass reduction = (36 kg/d ÷ 216 kg/d) × 100% = 16.7%, rounded.

**Step 7: calculate the change in normalized use.**

Normalized increase = 20 mg/L − 18 mg/L = 2 mg/L.

Relative normalized increase = (2 mg/L ÷ 18 mg/L) × 100% = 11.1%, rounded.

**Answer:** daily consumption decreased by approximately 16.7%, but chemical mass per treated volume increased by approximately 11.1%. A claim of improved chemical-use efficiency is unsupported by these figures.

This calculation is a period-average reconciliation, not proof of the instantaneous applied dose. Inventory timing, feed calibration, concentration changes, transfers and flow-meter error can affect it. A partial-day chemical total divided by a full-day flow total is invalid. Retain the inventory reconciliation, concentration basis, delivery and transfer records, calibrated feed information and flow-total timestamps.

If treatment performance improved while normalized use increased, the trial may identify a treatment benefit with a resource trade-off. Describe both. A more demanding source-water condition might justify further comparison, but it does not erase the measured increase.

### Review every barrier and prepare an evidence-based handover

Follow the changed water through the treatment train. Lower settled-water turbidity may reduce filter solids loading, but it does not guarantee better filter performance. Changes in particle characteristics, carryover or chemistry may affect filter ripening, breakthrough, headloss growth and run length differently.

Review individual filters as well as combined output. Compare similar positions within filter runs and record backwash events. A freshly washed filter and a late-run filter are not equivalent comparison units. If production flow changes, evaluate its effect on filter loading and hydraulic conditions before attributing the result to coagulation.

Disinfection requires its own aligned review. The **Procedure for Disinfection of Drinking Water (Ontario)** explains the CT concept, T10 and disinfectant-specific treatment requirements. CT depends on disinfectant, temperature, pH, residual and the approved hydraulic basis for the configuration. Use the applicable facility approval and validated procedure to establish the required comparison. Nominal tank volume divided by flow is not automatically an acceptable T10.

A residual from another interval cannot close the trial's disinfection review. Neither can a hydraulic assessment for a different tank arrangement. Where relevant conditions change, reassess the evidence under the approved basis. Do not assign treatment credit from settled-water improvement alone.

Measurement quality is part of this barrier review. **US EPA: Generating high-quality turbidity data**, EPA 815-B-19-010, is United States technical guidance, not Ontario law. Its measurement-chain and SCADA guidance supports checking the path from sample withdrawal through analyser output to the archived value. Sample-line delay, bubbles, fouling, maintenance modes, scaling, timestamp errors and historian averaging can distort a comparison.

**US EPA: Field turbidity measurement** is also United States technical guidance, not Ontario law. Local laboratory and site methods govern its use. A field check needs the specified sampling, handling and quality-control records. A grab sample and an online reading may differ because they represent different water or times. Investigate that mismatch rather than automatically choosing the lower result.

A handover should state the authorized trial status, current condition, elapsed process-response stage, outstanding samples, quality concerns and applicable stop criteria. Identify who owns each unresolved check. Include the approved reversion reference and any restrictions on further changes.

Close with a bounded conclusion: observed benefit, comparison limitations, barrier findings and next proposed review. An unresolved downstream record means the all-barriers conclusion remains open. It should not disappear into a footnote beneath a success headline.

### Common errors

- **Changing the acceptance rule after seeing the result.** This rewards favourable selection rather than testing the original question. Preserve the original rule and label any additional analysis as exploratory.
- **Treating missing or frozen data as stable operation.** Repeated values may reflect a historian or analyser problem. Check raw instrument status and quality flags before using them.
- **Comparing unmatched process periods.** Different source conditions, flows or filter-run stages can explain the apparent benefit. Arithmetic does not repair a poor comparison.
- **Calling reduced daily chemical mass an efficiency gain.** Lower production can reduce total consumption while mass per treated volume rises. Reconcile time windows and chemical basis first.
- **Using a downstream result from another configuration.** A disinfection review must represent the relevant water, conditions and approved hydraulic basis. A convenient earlier calculation is not transferable evidence.

### What to verify before you act

For an actual facility, consult the documents below through the site's authorization process. This lesson does not authorize a trial or replace operating and compliance instructions.

**Applicable approval and governing requirements.** Verify the Drinking Water Works Permit, Municipal Drinking Water Licence, applicable approval conditions and current Ontario requirements relevant to the proposed change. Establish whether the trial is within the authorized treatment configuration and delegated authority. Do not assume that a temporary change is exempt from review.

**Approved trial plan and operating procedures.** Confirm the proposed variable, permitted scope, acceptance criteria, stop criteria, stabilization basis, observation coverage, escalation contacts and reversion procedure. Identify who may authorize an extension or adopt a new condition. A trial result is evidence for review, not automatic permission for permanent adoption.

**Sampling and measurement records.** Consult the site sampling plan, instrument procedures, calibration and verification records, laboratory methods and SCADA tag definitions. Confirm units, location, timestamp convention, aggregation and quality flags. Retain original records alongside corrected datasets, with explanations for changes and exclusions.

**Disinfection records.** Verify the applicable disinfection procedure, approved hydraulic assessment, configuration record and time-aligned residual, flow, temperature and pH data. Use the **Procedure for Disinfection of Drinking Water (Ontario)** within that facility-specific framework. Resolve missing configuration evidence before claiming preserved treatment credit.

**Response and reporting procedures.** Trial review does not replace normal response duties. In Ontario, adverse drinking water test results require an immediate verbal report, followed by written notice within 24 hours after that report. Consult the applicable Ontario requirements and the site's current reporting procedure for recipients, responsibilities and required information.

**Final decision record.** Preserve the signed plan, raw evidence, calculations, deviations, cross-barrier assessment and handover. State what the evidence supports, what remains unresolved and who must review the next proposed step. If a condition changes, identify which comparisons and approvals require reconsideration rather than carrying the previous conclusion forward unchanged.

### Fictional worked scenario: defend a limited conclusion

The facility, operators, records and readings in this scenario are fictional. All numerical values and criteria are supplied case assumptions for a non-credit training exercise, not authorized operating values.

Cedar Point's draft study plan defines a primary learning criterion of at least 15% lower arithmetic mean settled-water turbidity, with separate filtration and disinfection reviews required. Eligible baseline readings are 0.70 NTU and 0.90 NTU. Eligible candidate readings are 0.55 NTU and 0.65 NTU. The fictional quality register documents satisfactory measurement checks and comparable source conditions.

The flow historian shows baseline production of 10,000 m³/d and candidate production of 8,000 m³/d. A summary note says, 'Flow unchanged; candidate alone caused improvement; all barriers passed.' Its attached disinfection calculation represents an earlier interval and a different tank configuration. The learner must reject the unsupported conclusions in that note while retaining it in the audit trail.

**Worked solution**

Baseline sum = 0.70 NTU + 0.90 NTU = 1.60 NTU.

Baseline mean = 1.60 NTU ÷ 2 = 0.80 NTU.

Candidate sum = 0.55 NTU + 0.65 NTU = 1.20 NTU.

Candidate mean = 1.20 NTU ÷ 2 = 0.60 NTU.

Absolute reduction = 0.80 NTU − 0.60 NTU = 0.20 NTU.

Relative reduction = (0.20 NTU ÷ 0.80 NTU) × 100% = 25%.

Flow decrease = 10,000 m³/d − 8,000 m³/d = 2,000 m³/d.

Relative flow decrease = (2,000 m³/d ÷ 10,000 m³/d) × 100% = 20%.

**Answer:** the observed 25% reduction meets the supplied primary criterion, but the 20% flow decrease confounds attribution. Overall success remains unproven. Consistent with the **Procedure for Disinfection of Drinking Water (Ontario)**, the disinfection review needs condition-specific evidence and the approved hydraulic basis for the actual configuration. Retain the historian export, quality register, conflicting note and calculation. Handover must identify the unresolved filtration and disinfection reviews and refer further action to the authorized trial procedure.
modules.assignment: Produce a trial review containing a normalized dose comparison, a cross-barrier evidence table and a critique of the draft claim. Design the next controlled comparison with baseline, source characterization, response lag, sampling plan, authorization, acceptance criteria and stop/escalation rules. Submit an 800–1,200-word protocol and handover plus calculations. Defend one alternative explanation in the instructor debrief.
rubric: Calculates 15 mg/L in both intervals; lower mass rate tracks lower flow and does not establish lower dose.
Separates observed settled-water improvement from temperature/flow confounding and unresolved Filter 2 behavior.
Provides prospective whole-train criteria, timing, authority and evidence retention; avoids unsupported all-barriers success.
modules.facilitatorGuide: Expected dose 4.5/300 × 1000 = 15 and 3.6/240 × 1000 = 15 mg/L. The claimed efficiency conclusion is unsupported. Require a meaningful proposal for aligning conditions and observing downstream response. Ask what would justify an inconclusive result; do not reward a learner solely for naming a preferred candidate.

activities.instruction: Study the lesson and reconstruct its worked example without looking at the solution.
Read the indicated source sections. Record the section used and one limitation on applying it to this case.
Analyse the supplied evidence, complete the written assignment and check units, timestamps and assumptions.
Compare one decision with an alternative interpretation, then self-check it against the case evidence and exercise feedback. Optional notes can capture your reasoning; count only active work.
Complete the module checks and final assessment; the course evaluation is optional. Review the automatic case feedback to address remaining questions.

checks.prompt: Non-credit study only, not operating or compliance instruction. When designing an optimization trial, how should success, protection and data-quality criteria relate?
choices: Define them separately before candidate observations begin.
Rank them after the trial according to the strongest measured benefit.
Use protection criteria alone to determine trial success.
Combine them into a single average-performance target.
checks.explanation: Separate prospective criteria distinguish observed benefit, barrier protection and interpretable evidence. Protection criteria alone cannot establish that the intended benefit occurred. Source: supplied module, 'Set acceptance, stop and data-quality criteria in advance'.

checks.prompt: Which approach provides the most defensible baseline for an optimization trial?
choices: Pool all archived readings without separating operating states or measurement quality.
Use representative intervals selected through the facility's validated sampling plan.
Choose the recent interval with the lowest settled-water turbidity.
Select the most stable interval from the previous shift.
checks.explanation: A baseline should represent relevant process conditions and variation through the validated sampling plan. A particularly stable interval may look attractive but can exclude the variation the comparison needs to represent. Source: supplied module, 'Frame a trial that can answer a specific question'.

checks.prompt: A fictional laboratory screening test improves settled-water turbidity. Which conclusion respects the test's unit of comparison?
choices: The result demonstrates that full-scale contact hydraulics will remain adequate.
The result justifies replacing the plant baseline.
The result supports a hypothesis needing full-scale barrier evaluation.
The result establishes acceptable performance across the treatment train.
checks.explanation: Laboratory screening can support a hypothesis, but it cannot establish full-scale hydraulics or downstream performance. Extending a bench result to the entire treatment train exceeds what the comparison measures. Source: supplied module, 'Frame a trial that can answer a specific question'.

checks.prompt: A fictional trial includes backwash-recovery observations. What is the strongest approach to deciding whether these observations enter the primary comparison?
choices: Exclude recovery observations whenever they increase the candidate mean.
Include every recovery observation without considering the comparison design.
Retain only recovery observations that resemble the baseline's most stable operating period.
Apply prospective transient rules and retain the documented basis for exclusions.
checks.explanation: Prospective rules prevent favourable results from determining which observations count. Excluding recovery observations merely because they worsen the mean introduces selection bias rather than a defensible quality decision. Source: supplied module, 'Set acceptance, stop and data-quality criteria in advance'.

checks.prompt: A fictional trial report shows a lower candidate mean but omits the time sequence. What additional evidence best addresses the limitations of that average?
choices: The raw sequence and the prospectively selected deterioration measures.
A recalculated mean using only observations below the original candidate mean.
The total number of readings collected during each condition.
The lowest candidate value and its corresponding timestamp.
checks.explanation: The sequence and planned peak, duration or variability measures can reveal deterioration hidden by an average. A large reading count does not reveal those events and may include strongly related observations. Source: supplied module, 'Worked example: calculate improvement without overstating causation'.

checks.prompt: What should determine when downstream observations become eligible after a fictional upstream treatment change?
choices: The start of the next shift, applied equally to every monitoring location.
The site's documented process response and appropriate hydraulic assessment.
The time when the chemical feed display first confirms the change.
The first downstream reading that favours the candidate.
checks.explanation: Eligibility must reflect the site's documented response and hydraulic understanding. Confirmation of an upstream feed change does not establish that the changed condition has reached every downstream monitoring point. Source: supplied module, 'Set acceptance, stop and data-quality criteria in advance'.

finalAssessment.prompt: Fictional case, supplied assumptions: a stream delivers 1,200 m³ at 10 mg/L suspended solids, then 800 m³ at 30 mg/L. Each concentration represents its entire interval. What suspended-solids mass passes during the combined interval?
choices: 36 kg of suspended solids.
18 kg of suspended solids for the interval.
24 kg of solids.
40 kg of suspended solids in total.
finalAssessment.explanation: Calculate the interval masses separately: 1,200 × 10 ÷ 1,000 = 12 kg and 800 × 30 ÷ 1,000 = 24 kg. Their sum is 36 kg. The tempting 40 kg answer applies the unweighted concentration average to unequal water volumes. Source: supplied module, 'Build an input register that preserves the evidence'. These fictional values are teaching assumptions only.

finalAssessment.prompt: Fictional case, supplied daily assumptions: plant input is 5,000 m³, finished output 5,100 m³, waste output 80 m³, and storage falls 200 m³. An internal recycle moves 100 m³. What is the whole-plant unexplained residual?
choices: −380 m³ remains as the unexplained whole-plant balance residual.
20 m³ remains as the unexplained balance residual.
120 m³ remains as the unexplained balance residual.
−180 m³ remains as an unexplained residual.
finalAssessment.explanation: The storage increase is −200 m³, so the residual is 5,000 − 5,100 − 80 − (−200) = 20 m³. Internal recycle is excluded. The 120 m³ answer incorrectly adds that recycle as new input. A residual identifies an investigation need, not necessarily a leak. Source: supplied module, 'Draw the boundary before calculating'. All quantities are fictional supplied assumptions.

finalAssessment.prompt: Fictional case, supplied assumptions: a downstream analyser displays a result at 11:20. Sample transport takes 6 min; upstream-to-downstream water travel takes 24 min. Clocks agree and no other lag applies. Which upstream passage time corresponds to this result?
choices: 11:14 at the upstream sampling location for this result.
10:44 at the upstream tap.
10:50 at the upstream sampling location.
10:56 at the upstream sampling location.
finalAssessment.explanation: Work backwards through both delays: 11:20 minus 6 min identifies downstream process passage at 11:14, then minus 24 min gives upstream passage at 10:50. The 10:56 answer subtracts only hydraulic travel and overlooks sample transport. Source: supplied module objective on hydraulic alignment and 'Build an input register that preserves the evidence'. The travel times and readings are fictional assumptions, not a validated hydraulic basis.

finalAssessment.prompt: Fictional case, supplied assumptions: a displayed residual meets the local optimisation target. The applicable validated procedure excludes the current contact configuration, and no supporting approval is documented. Which study conclusion is justified?
choices: Treat the target result as sufficient once a second residual reading confirms it.
Record target achievement and extend the earlier validation using unchanged nominal tank volume.
Treat the target result as evidence that validation extends to the current arrangement.
Record target achievement, but do not infer that the validated requirement is satisfied.
finalAssessment.explanation: Meeting an optimisation target does not establish satisfaction of a validated requirement outside the procedure's supported configuration. A second residual reading cannot establish missing hydraulic validation. CT is condition specific and depends on disinfectant, temperature, pH, residual and the approved hydraulic basis for the configuration. Source: supplied module objective distinguishing operating targets from validated treatment requirements. This fictional scenario is for study, not a compliance determination.

finalAssessment.prompt: Fictional case, supplied calculation assumptions: an inventory balance needs 6 kg of active ingredient. Product contains 25% active ingredient by mass and has density 1.20 kg/L. What product volume contains that mass? This is not an authorised feed quantity.
choices: 20 L of commercial product.
28.8 L of commercial product for the balance.
24 L of commercial product in total.
5 L of product.
finalAssessment.explanation: Required product mass is 6 ÷ 0.25 = 24 kg. Product volume is 24 ÷ 1.20 = 20 L. The 24 L distractor mistakes product mass for volume and effectively assumes a density of 1 kg/L. Source: supplied module, 'Worked example: convert flow and follow suspended-solids mass', chemical-product discussion. Actual calculation inputs require applicable supplier documentation and the validated feed-calibration procedure.

finalAssessment.prompt: Fictional training case, supplied assumptions: A and B each have 23 NTU. Alkalinity is 58 and 26 mg/L as CaCO3; temperatures are 12 and 4 °C, respectively. Each loses 18 mg/L as CaCO3 in a simplified balance. Which interpretation best sets test priorities?
choices: A retains 40 and B 8 mg/L as CaCO3; equal turbidity supports identical bench conditions.
A retains 40 and B 8 mg/L as CaCO3; B warrants buffering and cold-water checks.
A retains 76 and B 44 mg/L as CaCO3; B warrants buffering and cold-water checks.
A retains 40 and B 8 mg/L as CaCO3; both therefore have adequate buffering.
finalAssessment.explanation: Subtracting the supplied consumption gives 58 minus 18 equals 40 mg/L and 26 minus 18 equals 8 mg/L, both as CaCO3. B has less remaining reserve and is colder, supporting targeted investigation of both factors. Equal turbidity does not justify identical bench conditions, and the example establishes no authorised minimum alkalinity.

finalAssessment.prompt: Fictional training case, supplied assumptions: an intake event is stamped 10:06 by a clock running 6 min fast. Documented travel to the filter is 35 to 50 min for this configuration. All records use the same time zone. Which filter comparison window best matches the event?
choices: 10:00 to 10:15, after correcting the clock without adding travel.
10:29 to 10:44, after subtracting the clock offset again during alignment.
10:35 to 10:50, after correcting the clock and allowing for travel.
10:41 to 10:56, after using the stored timestamp and allowing for travel.
finalAssessment.explanation: The corrected intake event time is 10:00. Adding the supplied travel range gives 10:35 to 10:50. The tempting 10:41 to 10:56 window fails to correct the fast clock. This follows the module's timing-alignment approach and is not a disinfection contact-time determination.

finalAssessment.prompt: Fictional training case: paired intake samples have stable DOC but higher ultraviolet absorbance, with unchanged preparation and valid QC. Analysts propose changed organic character or increased total carbon. Which evidence package best separates these explanations?
choices: Repeat turbidity and apparent colour, then use agreement to infer a rise in total carbon.
Repeat DOC alone and use its stability to exclude any change in total organic carbon.
Compare historical feed rates and current absorbance, treating feed demand as a measure of total carbon.
Measure paired total organic carbon and method-matched absorbance, retaining sample fractions.
finalAssessment.explanation: The supplied module explains that DOC, total organic carbon and ultraviolet absorbance answer different questions. Total organic carbon addresses the proposed total-carbon increase, while matched absorbance retains evidence about light-absorbing character. Stable DOC alone cannot exclude a change in material outside the DOC fraction.

finalAssessment.prompt: Fictional training case: a raw-water trend spikes just after maintenance, while matched grabs remain steady. A brief source pulse and changed signal processing remain possible. Which review best distinguishes them?
choices: Compare original analyser output, processing settings, QC records and precise grab timing.
Compare the maintenance log with the displayed spike and attribute the spike to maintenance.
Compare the grab average with the trend maximum and retain whichever dataset has more readings.
Compare the daily mean with the previous day and accept a source pulse if the mean increased.
finalAssessment.explanation: Tracing original output through processing and checking grab timing can separate a missed brief pulse from a processing artefact. Maintenance coincidence alone does not prove causation. The module draws on US EPA's Generating high-quality turbidity data, EPA 815-B-19-010, as United States technical guidance, not Ontario law; facility procedures govern local use.

finalAssessment.prompt: Fictional training case: the current intake is cold, low in alkalinity and DOC-rich, with a fixed source blend. Archived periods all have similar turbidity. Which period offers the most defensible source-characterisation comparison?
choices: A cold period with matching alkalinity, changed blending and only an overall daily DOC mean.
A cold period with matching alkalinity, DOC, blending and comparable analytical methods.
A cold period with matching DOC and blending, but higher alkalinity and a matching chemical-feed trend.
A warmer period with matching DOC, fixed blending and clearly documented analytical methods.
finalAssessment.explanation: The selected period matches the relevant source properties, configuration and analytical basis. The supplied module warns that similar turbidity or chemical-feed history does not establish similar buffering or treatability. A daily mean across a blend change also weakens the comparison.

finalAssessment.prompt: Fictional supplied assumptions: matched interval totals are 18.0 L of coagulant and 300 m³ of water. Density is 1.25 kg/L and strength is 8.00% by mass as Al₂O₃ equivalent. What interval active dose follows from these totals?
choices: 75 mg/L as Al₂O₃ equivalent.
0.600 mg/L as Al₂O₃ equivalent.
6.00 mg/L as Al₂O₃ equivalent.
60.0 mg/L as Al₂O₃ equivalent.
finalAssessment.explanation: The active mass is 18.0 × 1.25 × 0.0800 = 1.80 kg. Dividing by the matched 300 m³ gives 6.00 mg/L as Al₂O₃ equivalent. The 75 mg/L alternative is the product-mass dose and omits the strength conversion. This follows the supplied module's matched-total calculation basis.

finalAssessment.prompt: Fictional supplied assumptions: at constant water flow, an old product feeds at 8.00 L/h, density 1.20 kg/L and 12.0% by mass as Al₂O₃ equivalent. A replacement has density 1.25 kg/L and 10.0% on the same basis. Which calculated feed preserves active dose, rounded to 0.01 L/h?
choices: 9.6 L/h of replacement product.
8.000 L/h of replacement product.
7.68 L/h of replacement product.
9.22 L/h of replacement product.
finalAssessment.explanation: The old active mass rate is 8.00 × 1.20 × 0.120 = 1.152 kg/h. The replacement supplies 1.25 × 0.100 = 0.125 kg active/L, so the calculated equivalent feed is 9.216 L/h, rounded to 9.22 L/h. The 9.6 L/h alternative adjusts strength but ignores the density change. This is an accounting comparison, not an authorised pump setting.

finalAssessment.prompt: Fictional supplied screen: mean ≤0.60 NTU, range ≤0.08 NTU, every pH 6.6 to 7.0. X: turbidity 0.48/0.60 NTU, pH 6.8/6.9. Y: turbidity 0.55/0.59 NTU, pH 6.7/6.8. Which conclusion follows?
choices: Only Y meets the screen because X exceeds the turbidity range criterion.
Only X meets the screen because its lower mean establishes better consistency.
Both meet the screen because each mean and every pH meet their criteria.
Neither meets the screen because both turbidity pairs show variation.
finalAssessment.explanation: X has mean turbidity 0.54 NTU but range 0.12 NTU, exceeding the supplied exercise criterion. Y has mean 0.57 NTU and range 0.04 NTU, with both pH results within the supplied range. Selecting X for its lower mean ignores consistency. These are fictional comparison criteria, not drinking-water standards.

finalAssessment.prompt: In a fictional study, candidate jars outperform baseline jars, but the candidate jars received a different settling time. Instrument checks passed. What evidence plan best addresses whether dose caused the improvement?
choices: Compare the existing averages and retain the condition with lower turbidity.
Repeat independent jars with matched settling and other bench conditions.
Apply a settling-time correction to every result using the observed difference.
Repeat readings of the stored samples to narrow instrument uncertainty.
finalAssessment.explanation: The supplied module requires controlled bench conditions. Different settling times confound the dose comparison, so independent preparations under matched conditions address the treatment question. Re-reading stored samples cannot remove the original settling-time difference, even when instrument checks pass.

finalAssessment.prompt: A fictional study has verified product strength, measured delivery and repeatable candidate performance. Downstream response remains uncertain. Which proposed trial package best supports site review without treating the bench result as authorisation?
choices: Site-reviewed dose bounds and a closing summary using routine downstream records.
A candidate dose, routine sampling, and trial completion whenever average turbidity improves.
Site-approved bounds, matched monitoring, downstream checks, stop/revert criteria and review.
A candidate dose, enhanced settled-water checks, and wider changes if the trend remains favourable.
finalAssessment.explanation: A bounded proposal needs site-reviewed limits, a traceable monitoring basis, downstream assessment, stop/revert criteria and review against the facility approval and validated procedures. Dose bounds and a closing summary alone leave response to deterioration undefined. Bench success supports review but does not authorise a plant change.

finalAssessment.prompt: Fictional study assumptions: active areas A = 20 m², B = 30 m². Stable filtration flows change from A/B = 100/240 to 160/180 m³/h at matched run stages. Which loading summary is supported, without judging acceptability?
choices: Afterwards, A = 8.0 m/h and B = 6.0 m/h; aggregate rises to 7.0 m/h overall.
Afterwards, A = 5.0 m/h and B = 8.0 m/h; aggregate is 6.8 m/h.
Afterwards, A = 6.0 m/h and B = 8.0 m/h; aggregate remains at 6.8 m/h overall.
Afterwards, A = 8.0 m/h and B = 6.0 m/h; aggregate stays at 6.8 m/h.
finalAssessment.explanation: Using the supplied module's Q/area method, the new unit loadings are 160/20 = 8.0 m/h and 180/30 = 6.0 m/h. Total flow remains 340 m³/h over 50 m², giving 6.8 m/h. Averaging the two unit loadings gives 7.0 m/h but incorrectly weights unequal areas equally. These assumptions establish no authorised loading.

finalAssessment.prompt: Fictional study assumptions: at run ages 3–7 h, A's headloss rises from 0.40 to 1.00 m and B's from 0.60 to 1.40 m. Both have stable loading of 5.0 m/h and valid, equivalent instruments. What are their average headloss accumulation rates and difference?
choices: A: 0.15 m/h; B: 0.20 m/h; difference: 0.05 m/h.
A: 0.25 m/h; B: 0.35 m/h; difference: 0.10 m/h.
A: 0.086 m/h; B: 0.114 m/h; difference: 0.028 m/h.
finalAssessment.explanation: The common interval is 7 − 3 = 4 h. A accumulates (1.00 − 0.40)/4 = 0.15 m/h and B accumulates (1.40 − 0.60)/4 = 0.20 m/h. Their difference is 0.05 m/h. Dividing endpoint headloss by duration incorrectly includes headloss already present at the interval's start. The supplied module cautions that unequal rates do not identify a cause.

finalAssessment.prompt: Fictional study records: clarified-water turbidity rises before both filters respond, allowing for verified travel times. After upstream recovery, only B remains elevated. Loading and run stage are matched; analyzers are valid. Which interpretation best fits?
choices: B's persistent response proves a bed defect caused both filters' initial rise.
A shared initial influence is supported; B's persistence needs unit-specific review.
The shared initial rise establishes that B has no filter-specific issue to investigate.
Matching loading establishes that the upstream event explains B's full response.
finalAssessment.explanation: The sequence supports a shared upstream influence initially, while B's persistence under matched conditions supports additional unit-specific investigation. The supplied module requires separating observation from explanation. The common initial response does not rule out a later or additional issue in B.

finalAssessment.prompt: Fictional study assumptions: valid 10 s turbidity records contain a 40 s rise during steady filtration. A proposed report retains only 15 min means. Which study record best preserves evidence for later review?
choices: Keep interval means and the maximum value; omit event timing once the peak is recorded.
Keep the event plot and interval means; discard source records after checking the image.
Keep detailed records, flags and state changes; use interval means as additional context.
Keep detailed records only above the event peak; retain means for all remaining periods.
finalAssessment.explanation: Detailed records preserve event timing, duration and context; flags and operating state preserve interpretability. Means can conceal a short rise, and a maximum alone loses duration and sequence. This follows the supplied module's requirement to preserve short-duration changes rather than conceal them inside averages. The stated intervals are teaching assumptions, not monitoring requirements.

finalAssessment.prompt: Fictional study assumptions: a turbidity rise appears 2 min before a flow step. Analyzer and flow clocks are unverified; nearby turbidity records carry a maintenance flag. What is the strongest next analytical step?
choices: Use the apparent event order to exclude the flow step, then examine upstream records.
Shift turbidity to follow the flow step, retaining the flagged values as process evidence.
Remove the flagged values permanently, then treat the remaining clock order as verified.
Retain original records, verify time bases and flags, then reassess the event sequence.
finalAssessment.explanation: The supplied module's input register requires clock alignment and an understanding of data validity before interpreting event order. Preserving originals supports review of any subsequent correction. The apparent lead cannot exclude a flow-related explanation while clocks and maintenance effects remain unresolved.

finalAssessment.prompt: Fictional supplied assumptions: working volume 480 m³, flow 360 m³/h, supported T10 factor 0.50 (dimensionless), endpoint free-chlorine residual 0.75 mg/L and condition-matched criterion 25 mg·min/L. With T10 = (volume/flow) × factor, which CT and ratio follow?
choices: CT is 30 mg·min/L, giving a ratio of 1.20.
CT is 22.5 mg·min/L, giving a ratio of 0.90.
CT is 60 mg·min/L, giving a ratio of 2.4.
CT is 0.50 mg·min/L, giving a ratio of 0.020.
finalAssessment.explanation: Flow is 6 m³/min, nominal time is 80 min, T10 is 40 min and CT is 30 mg·min/L. Dividing by the supplied criterion gives 1.20. The 60 mg·min/L distractor incorrectly uses nominal time. Source: supplied module's CT and hydraulic-factor relationships. These fictional assumptions support non-credit study only, not operating or compliance decisions.

finalAssessment.prompt: Fictional supplied assumptions: branch A has working volume 180 m³ and flow 360 m³/h. Combined branches have 600 m³ and 600 m³/h. Branch A's supported T10/nominal-time factor is 0.40 (dimensionless). Which nominal time and T10 apply to branch A?
choices: Nominal time is 30 min; T10 is 30 min.
Nominal time is 30 min; T10 is 12.0 min.
Nominal time is 18.0 min; T10 is 7.20 min.
Nominal time is 60.0 min; T10 is 24.0 min.
finalAssessment.explanation: Branch A flow is 6 m³/min, so its nominal time is 180/6 = 30 min and T10 is 30 × 0.40 = 12 min. Combining branch volumes and flows gives a different result that cannot establish branch A's performance. Source: supplied module, parallel branches and effective-time calculation.

finalAssessment.prompt: After level falls and flow rises, fictional supplied assumptions are volume 360 m³, flow 540 m³/h, endpoint free-chlorine residual 0.80 mg/L and condition-matched criterion 20 mg·min/L. T10 = (volume/flow) × 0.50 remains supported; the factor is dimensionless. Which result follows?
choices: CT is 0.267 mg·min/L, giving a ratio of 0.0133.
CT is 20 mg·min/L, giving a ratio of 1.00.
CT is 16 mg·min/L, giving a ratio of 0.80.
CT is 32 mg·min/L, giving a ratio of 1.6.
finalAssessment.explanation: Flow is 9 m³/min, nominal time is 40 min, T10 is 20 min and CT is 16 mg·min/L. The ratio is 0.80 against this case criterion. A CT of 32 uses nominal time instead of effective time. Source: supplied module, reassessment after changed flow and working volume. Hydraulic support at the changed condition is an explicit case assumption.

finalAssessment.prompt: Fictional supplied assumptions: a free-chlorine CT ratio was 1.30 at 15 °C and pH 7.0 (dimensionless). Temperature is now 5 °C and pH 8.0; residual and supported T10 are unchanged. No criterion for the new chemistry is supplied. Which conclusion is justified?
choices: The earlier ratio remains valid because residual and T10 are unchanged.
The earlier ratio becomes conservative because colder water retains chlorine longer.
The earlier ratio can be corrected using only the proportional temperature change.
The earlier ratio cannot establish the comparison under the changed chemistry.
finalAssessment.explanation: The calculated C × T10 may be unchanged, but the applicable criterion must match the new temperature and pH as well as disinfectant and treatment objective. Reusing the earlier ratio ignores that dependency. Source: supplied module and Ontario's Procedure for Disinfection of Drinking Water. The case supplies no basis for a numerical correction.

finalAssessment.prompt: Fictional supplied assumptions: an endpoint analyser displays a residual at 10:06; sample transport takes 6 min. Clocks agree. The case-validated alignment method subtracts transport delay to select contemporaneous flow and level records. Which record time belongs with this residual?
choices: Use 10:00, accounting for sample transport.
Use 10:12, adding the sample transport delay.
Use 09:54, allowing twice for sample transport delay.
Use 10:06, matching the analyser display.
finalAssessment.explanation: Subtracting the supplied 6 min delay from 10:06 gives 10:00 under this case's validated alignment method. Matching displayed timestamps would pair the residual with a later process interval. Source: supplied module, time alignment. Real alignment must follow the facility's validated method rather than an invented shift.

finalAssessment.prompt: Fictional supplied case assumptions, not authorized values: eligible baseline turbidity is 0.90, 1.10 NTU; candidate is 0.72, 0.88 NTU. The primary criterion is at least 15% mean reduction. Disinfection review is incomplete. Which assessment is justified?
choices: The reduction is 25%; the primary criterion is met, but disinfection evidence still prevents an overall conclusion.
The reduction is 20%; the primary criterion is met, but all-barriers success remains unestablished.
The reduction is 10%; the primary criterion is missed and the candidate should be classified as ineffective.
The reduction is 20%; all-barriers success is established.
finalAssessment.explanation: The means are 1.00 and 0.80 NTU. The reduction is (1.00 − 0.80) ÷ 1.00 × 100% = 20%, exceeding the supplied criterion by 5 percentage points. Dividing by the candidate mean gives the tempting but incorrect 25%. An incomplete disinfection review prevents an all-barriers success claim. Source: supplied module, worked example and decision register.

finalAssessment.prompt: In a fictional authorized comparison, source turbidity falls as the candidate begins. Settled-water turbidity improves and stays improved after a planned return to baseline. Eligible windows and instrument checks are valid. Which interpretation is strongest?
choices: Treat the return result as proof that the candidate has a persistent benefit after withdrawal.
Reject the observed improvement entirely because the source-water conditions changed during the comparison.
Report the improvement, identify the source trend, and seek a more comparable contrast.
Credit the candidate because improvement began during its use.
finalAssessment.explanation: The improvement is a valid observation, but its persistence after returning to baseline is consistent with a source-water trend. The timing of the initial improvement alone does not establish candidate causation, and confounding does not erase the measured observation. Source: supplied module, 'Frame a trial that can answer a specific question'.

finalAssessment.prompt: Fictional records show the primary outcome met. An individual filter crosses its trial-specific interruption criterion, although combined filtrate remains stable. The facility-approved trial plan requires interruption and escalation for that event. Which assessment fits?
choices: Recommend continuation because the combined result remains stable.
Classify the trial as inconclusive solely because the combined result differs from the individual-filter trend.
Classify the trial as successful but record the filter event for discussion at the next routine review.
Record the primary benefit, reject overall success, and refer to the plan's interruption and escalation response.
finalAssessment.explanation: Meeting the primary outcome does not override an individual-filter protection criterion. The assessment must preserve both findings and point to the facility-approved response. Stable combined filtrate can conceal a deteriorating filter. Source: supplied module, decision register, 'Filter protection'.

finalAssessment.prompt: A fictional trial reaches its planned endpoint. Candidate readings look favourable, but a required analyser check failed and the plan provides no validated substitute. An extension is proposed solely to obtain a passing result. Which recommendation is defensible?
choices: Classify the comparison as inconclusive; retain the endpoint and require authorization and rationale for any extension.
Accept the favourable readings because failure of the analyser check does not itself establish that treatment performance deteriorated.
Discard flagged readings and continue collecting until the acceptance criterion is met.
Declare treatment failure and combine any extension readings with the original trial.
finalAssessment.explanation: Failed required quality checks can make evidence uninterpretable without proving treatment failure. Extending only to obtain a favourable result biases the comparison. The original endpoint must remain identifiable, and any extension needs its own authorization and rationale. Source: supplied module, 'Set acceptance, stop and data-quality criteria in advance'.

finalAssessment.prompt: In a fictional trial handover, settled-water results improve. Disinfectant residual is unchanged, but flow and contact configuration differ from baseline. What handover entry best supports a defensible cross-barrier review?
choices: Report unchanged residual as sufficient evidence of equivalent disinfection, with configuration details available on request.
Flag disinfection as unresolved; retain condition and hydraulic records, and identify review, escalation and reversion owners.
Flag disinfection for review but leave ownership to the incoming shift.
Report improved turbidity and carry forward the previous CT assessment.
finalAssessment.explanation: Unchanged residual does not establish equivalent CT performance after flow or configuration changes. Review depends on disinfectant, temperature, pH, residual and the approved hydraulic basis for the configuration. Handover also needs clear responsibilities, not merely an unresolved flag. Source: supplied module, decision register, 'Disinfection protection' and 'Trial ownership'.
